messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan's life was forever changed when he was diagnosed with leukemia two years ago. He remembered the hospital room where the doctor delivered the news, the fluorescent lights overhead, and the antiseptic smell that filled his nostrils. What struck him most was the feeling of his body betraying him, as if he had been living in a fragile shell all along. The grueling months of chemotherapy that followed only reinforced this notion - every session felt like a battle to reclaim control over his own flesh. As Rohan slowly began to recover, he found himself increasingly avoiding anything that reminded him of those harrowing days. Hospitals, ambulances, and even physical examinations became triggers that sent his mind racing back to the darkest moments of his illness. He would steer clear of conversations about health, medical dramas on TV, or even news articles about illnesses. His friends and family grew concerned about his newfound aversion to discussing his experience, but Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that revisiting those memories would somehow jinx his fragile recovery. At work, as a UX designer, Rohan's creativity began to suffer. He found himself constantly on edge, his body tense and ready to react to any perceived danger. Even minor setbacks in projects or delays in meeting deadlines made him assume the worst - that something was terribly wrong, just like it had been during his illness. His colleagues noticed a change in his demeanor, how he would bristle at suggestions or get defensive over feedback. Rohan knew this wasn't the person he used to be, but he couldn't seem to shake off the feeling of being on high alert all the time. Rohan's wife, Nalini, tried her best to reassure him that he was safe now, that the cancer was in remission, and that they would face any future challenges together. But Rohan just couldn't bring himself to believe it. There was a nagging voice inside his head, whispering that something was fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that he was weak and defective. This self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life - he felt emotionally numb, disconnected from the things that used to give him joy. As time went on, Rohan's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships. Nalini grew frustrated with his reluctance to discuss important health matters or make plans for their future together. His friends and family felt shut out by his unwillingness to engage in conversations about his experience. Even simple activities like going for a walk or trying new restaurants became sources of stress, as Rohan worried about putting his body under undue strain. One day, when Nalini confronted him about the growing distance between them, Rohan realized he couldn't keep living like this. The numbness and tension had become unbearable. He knew it was time to seek help, not just for himself but also for those who cared about him. As he sat in his therapist's office, filling out forms and answering questions, Rohan felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to reclaim control over his life and find a way to trust himself again. But as he left the office that day, Rohan couldn't shake off the familiar feeling of dread - what if seeking help was just another sign of weakness? What if he wasn't strong enough to overcome this? The fear swirled inside him like a living thing, a constant reminder of the long and difficult journey ahead.
